**Device Classification and Regulatory Pathways**

Under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR 2021/820) a prescription digital therapeutic (PDT) that is intended to diagnose, treat or manage a medical condition falls within the definition of a “medical device.”  The MDR classifies devices into Classes I, IIa, IIb and III on the basis of risk.  A PDT that delivers pharmacological‑grade instructions, modifies drug dosing or provides real‑time monitoring for chronic disease management is normally considered a Class IIa device; if it performs higher‑risk functions such as automated decision support for life‑supporting therapy, it may be escalated to Class IIb or III.  The manufacturer must therefore conduct a risk assessment in accordance with Annex III and prepare the appropriate technical documentation (Annex IV).  In the United Kingdom, post‑Brexit, the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002/2019 remain in force; the device is still classified under the same risk categories, but the conformity assessment route for Class IIa devices requires a notified body’s review of the clinical evaluation and quality management system.  The UK also retains the MDR‑derived “UKCA” marking regime for devices that are placed on the market after 1 January 2023; a dual CE/UKCA mark is often advisable to cover both markets.

**CE Marking, Post‑Market Surveillance and Vigilance**

To obtain a CE mark (or UKCA), the manufacturer must demonstrate compliance with the MDR’s essential requirements (Annex I) and provide evidence of clinical performance.  For Class IIa devices, the conformity assessment is performed by a notified body that issues a certificate after reviewing the technical file, risk management file, and quality system audit.  The device must also be registered in the European Database on Medical Devices (EUDAMED).  Post‑market surveillance obligations are codified in Annex V: the manufacturer must collect and analyse data on performance and adverse events, conduct periodic safety update reports (PSURs), and report serious incidents to competent authorities within 10 days.  In Germany, the Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices (BfArM) requires that Class IIa devices be listed in the “Medical Device Register” and that any changes to the product or its intended use trigger a re‑notification process.

**UK‑Specific Requirements: NICE Guidance and NHS Tariff**

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has issued guidance on digital therapeutics, including the “Digital Therapeutics Programme” and the “Clinical Effectiveness and Cost‑Effectiveness of Digital Interventions” framework.  A PDT must demonstrate clinical effectiveness, cost‑effectiveness, and alignment with NHS priorities to be considered for inclusion in the NHS tariff schedule.  The tariff mechanism requires that the device be listed on the NHS Digital Therapeutics Catalogue (if available) and that a “Digital Health Technology Assessment” (DHTA) is completed.  As of my knowledge cutoff in September 2023, NICE had published interim guidance for Class IIa digital therapeutics; however, updates to the tariff or the inclusion criteria may have occurred since then.  Manufacturers should consult the latest NICE Digital Therapeutic Programme documents and NHS Digital’s “Digital Health Technology Assessment” portal for current requirements.

**German‑Specific Requirements: G‑BA Reimbursement Criteria**

In Germany, prescription digital therapeutics can be pursued through the DiGA (Digitale Gesundheitsanwendungen) pathway administered by the Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss (G‑BA).  The device must satisfy three core criteria: (1) clinical benefit demonstrated in a prospective study or real‑world evidence; (2) data protection compliance, including GDPR and the Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (BDSG); and (3) technical feasibility for integration into the German health system.  Upon meeting these criteria, the manufacturer applies to BfArM for DiGA listing; successful applications result in reimbursement under statutory health insurance at a negotiated tariff.  The G‑BA’s “DiGA‑Guideline” (updated annually) specifies that the device must provide an electronic patient record and support interoperability with existing German eHealth standards (e.g., HL7 FHIR).  Since my training data end in September 2023, it is possible that the DiGA tariff rates or eligibility thresholds have been revised; manufacturers should verify current G‑BA documentation.

Under the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), a PDT processes personal data of patients and possibly health‑related data.
